question: What circuit lets a one-block transformer solve sparse modular addition, how does that circuit arise during optimization, and can its small-scale dynamics explain stage transitions and loss spikes seen in larger transformer training?

key_findings.claim: A clustering head is a sufficient circuit for the task, but stationarity is the only theoretical learning guarantee.
key_findings.evidence: The proposed circuit collapses informative position embeddings, suppresses or value-cancels suffix tokens, clusters sequences by the multiset of the first k token values, and lets the MLP map clusters to modular sums. Proposition 3 proves that an exact construction has zero population-loss gradient; it does not prove convergence to that circuit, local minimality, uniqueness, or stability.

key_findings.claim: Trained models implement several functionally equivalent rather than one canonical clustering circuit.
key_findings.evidence: The visual audit shows an ideal invariant circuit, attention errors repaired by the value map, partially invariant solutions with extra clusters, and fuzzy but generalizing partitions. Initial and final attention maps remain similar, so the selected realization depends strongly on initialization.

key_findings.claim: The observed learning trace has two ordered functional changes: sequence clustering and then MLP fitting.
key_findings.evidence: In the low-dimensional sandbox, the first loss drop coincides with a rapid reorganization of sequence embeddings after a plateau; the second coincides with fitting decision regions over those clusters. Layerwise gradient-norm bursts accompany the changes, but a near-zero gradient is only indirect evidence for a saddle rather than a measured Hessian diagnosis.

key_findings.claim: The gradient bound is descriptive, not a proof that optimization will remain stable.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4 upper-bounds the full gradient by a prediction-error factor times terms built from bounded embeddings and parameter spectral norms. Those parameter norms are themselves uncontrolled during training, and the result neither bounds curvature nor supplies a permitted step size.

key_findings.claim: Two visually diagnosed high-curvature mechanisms coincide with loss spikes.
key_findings.evidence: Near zero, x divided by its norm can change sharply when an update exceeds the input norm. Separately, heavy or highly correlated MLP weights place steep decision boundaries near a sequence embedding, so a small embedding move changes the prediction. Mini-batch plots show gradient- and loss-norm spikes together, but do not causally separate these mechanisms from batch noise or optimizer state.

key_findings.claim: Pretraining on binary addition can transfer a useful invariant circuit to larger vocabularies.
key_findings.evidence: With sequence length 12, 2,048 samples, and 1,000 epochs per stage, models pretrained at p=2 and fine-tuned at p=3 outperform models trained only at the harder vocabulary. Across more than 250 runs per bar, only models that formed the six ideal p=2 clusters reached 100% p=3 test accuracy; the study does not compare compute-matched longer direct training or natural curricula.

key_findings.claim: Successful solutions use denser GELU activations under the paper's thresholded sparsity measure.
key_findings.evidence: Across 20 models, runs above 0.9 test accuracy separate from failures over a useful epsilon range and have fewer near-zero activations. The trend repeats for embedding dimensions 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, and 32; at dimension 8 and above every sampled model succeeds, making causality between density and success unresolved.

key_findings.claim: The large-language-model implications remain hypotheses from a deliberately narrow testbed.
key_findings.evidence: The experiments train one simplified cross-attention block on one synthetic arithmetic distribution, mostly with two-dimensional embeddings. Higher-dimensional repeats preserve correlations between loss and gradient spikes, but the paper does not intervene on normalization, test its proposed smoothing, train a language model, or establish that the same circuit or causal spike source exists at scale.

method.core_idea: Make every component of a small transformer visually inspectable while training it on a task whose permutation and suffix invariances imply a concrete attention-and-MLP circuit.
method.mechanism: The model embeds tokens and positions, uses one cross-attention query to aggregate a length-12 sequence, applies a normalized GELU MLP and residual, and decodes with tied token embeddings. Closed-form gradients certify stationary clustering-head constructions. Training snapshots, attention maps, activation thresholds, gradient norms, curriculum transfers, and higher-dimensional repeats are used to interpret optimization.
assumptions: Sparse modular addition captures training phenomena relevant beyond its synthetic distribution.
The simplified one-block cross-attention architecture retains the mechanisms of interest.
Two-dimensional projections are faithful enough to classify circuit behavior.
Near-zero gradients during plateaus are adequate evidence for saddle-like dynamics.
Correlated loss and gradient spikes reveal the proposed high-curvature causes.
Fixed embeddings in the theory still illuminate experiments that train embeddings.

techniques.role: Turns permutation- and suffix-equivalent inputs into shared sequence representations.
Tracks embeddings, attention, value transforms, MLP regions, loss, and gradients in a common two-dimensional sandbox.
Uses exact derivatives to show that an ideal clustering circuit is a stationary population-loss point.
Transfers an invariant circuit learned on p=2 into a p=3 task.
Measures near-zero GELU activations across many thresholds instead of imposing a single sparsity cutoff.
Relates normalization and MLP geometry to abrupt loss changes.

evaluations.setting: Sparse modular addition with default N=12, k=5, p in {2,3}, one simplified transformer block, and 2^11 sampled training points
evaluations.metric: Train/test loss, accuracy, layer geometry, attention patterns, and gradient norms
evaluations.result: Multiple clustering-like circuits generalize; representative runs show a cluster-formation drop followed by MLP fitting and occasional loss spikes.
evaluations.baseline: Random initialization, failed runs, and idealized clustering-head geometry

evaluations.setting: Twenty independently trained models and epsilon from 10^-5 to 10^2
evaluations.metric: Fraction of near-zero GELU activations and test accuracy
evaluations.result: Runs above 0.9 test accuracy have consistently denser activations over the separating threshold range.
evaluations.baseline: Runs at or below 0.9 test accuracy

evaluations.setting: p=2 pretraining followed by p=3 fine-tuning, versus training on the harder vocabulary without the first stage
evaluations.metric: Mean and maximum test accuracy across more than 250 runs per configuration
evaluations.result: Transferred models perform better; perfect p=3 runs arise only when pretraining formed all six invariant p=2 clusters.
evaluations.baseline: Pretraining-only/direct-training configurations at each vocabulary size

evaluations.setting: Embedding dimensions 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, 32 and full- or mini-batch training
evaluations.metric: Loss/gradient spike alignment, two-stage traces, activation density, and success rate
evaluations.result: The reported correlations persist beyond dimension two; all sampled runs succeed from dimension eight in the sparsity study.

limitations: Only one synthetic task and one simplified transformer block are studied.
The stationary-point proof gives no convergence, stability, optimality, or circuit-selection guarantee.
The gradient bound depends on parameter norms that are not controlled by the result.
Loss-spike mechanisms are inferred visually without targeted causal interventions.
Most mechanistic evidence uses dimension two; higher-dimensional repeats expose only aggregate traces.
The curriculum comparison is not fully compute- and update-matched.
Thresholded activation density is correlational and task-specific.
No language-model pretraining experiment validates the proposed scale transfer.
failure_modes: A different initialization forms a partially invariant or unnecessarily complex decision partition.
A long plateau is mislabeled as a saddle when slow feature learning or optimizer state is responsible.
Near-zero normalized inputs amplify an update and cause a transient loss excursion.
Correlated MLP weights create a steep boundary close to a representation cluster.
A curriculum transfers a shortcut specialized to the source vocabulary instead of the intended invariant.
Denser activations correlate with greater capacity rather than causing correct circuit formation.
Mechanisms from a single cross-attention query fail to survive depth, self-attention, token diversity, or realistic data.
reusable_insights: Choose synthetic tasks with explicit invariances so learned circuits can be checked against necessary computations.
Treat functionally equivalent circuits as a distribution over solutions, not a single canonical mechanism.
Track internal progress measures alongside loss to distinguish representation formation from readout fitting.
Use interventions on suspected high-curvature components before extrapolating a visual correlation to scale.
Audit curricula by checking whether the intended invariant, rather than only accuracy, transfers.
Sweep sparsity thresholds and capacity so arbitrary cutoffs do not create a mechanism claim.
Separate a stationary construction from a theorem about learnability.
open_questions: Which stationary clustering heads are stable local minima, and which are reached with non-negligible probability?
Does smoothing RMSNorm near zero prevent spikes without harming expressivity or transfer?
Can causal Hessian-vector probes distinguish normalization, MLP-boundary, batch-noise, and optimizer-state spikes?
Do comparable representation-then-readout phases occur across layers in language-model pretraining?
How should circuit transfer be measured when source and target tasks admit different shortcuts?
Does activation density cause successful invariant computation after matching width and effective capacity?

competitive_landscape.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: Nanda and colleagues reverse-engineer Fourier circuits and divide grokking into memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. This paper uses sparse rather than standard modular addition, a cross-attention clustering circuit, and layer-by-layer geometric snapshots, but its two stages do not establish the predecessor's three-phase account is absent.

competitive_landscape.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
competitive_landscape.difference: Power et al. establish delayed generalization and dataset-size effects on modular tasks. The reviewed paper focuses on internal circuit formation, invariance transfer, and within-run loss spikes rather than delayed train-test generalization itself.

competitive_landscape.title: The merged-staircase property: a necessary and nearly sufficient condition for SGD learning of sparse functions on two-layer neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Abbe et al. characterize dimension-efficient SGD learnability of latent sparse Boolean functions in a mean-field two-layer network. The reviewed study instead analyzes one transformer on modular sparse inputs and proves only stationarity of a sufficient circuit.

competitive_landscape.title: Spike No More: Stabilizing the Pre-training of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Takase et al. derive small-sublayer and large-shortcut conditions and validate spike prevention in language-model pretraining. The reviewed paper offers more visually resolved hypotheses about normalization and MLP curvature but does not perform the corresponding large-scale intervention.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Empirical Interpretation of Internal Circuits and Properties in Grokked Transformers on Modular Polynomials
competitive_landscape.difference: Furuta et al. compare Fourier features, transfer, and multi-task co-grokking across several modular polynomials. The reviewed paper isolates sparse-addition invariances and optimization instability with a lower-dimensional visual sandbox.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Mechanism and Dynamics of Modular Addition: Fourier Features, Lottery Ticket, and Grokking
competitive_landscape.difference: He et al. prove frequency competition, phase symmetry, diversification, and a three-stage modular-addition account for two-layer networks. It supplies stronger circuit-selection dynamics for a different architecture; the reviewed clustering-head stationarity result still lacks such reachability theory.

novelty_assessment: The defensible novelty is the joint visual and analytic case study of a sparse-addition clustering circuit, including functionally equivalent realizations, circuit-level curriculum transfer, and candidate normalization/MLP spike mechanisms. Modular arithmetic circuits, grokking stages, sparse-function learnability, and transformer spike mitigation all predate it. Its strongest scale-facing claims are useful hypotheses, not demonstrations: the proof certifies stationary constructions, and the experiments do not causally validate the proposed spike sources or reproduce them in language-model pretraining.
reviewer_notes: Read all 44 cached pages, including the experimental appendix and full gradient/stationarity proofs. Visually inspected Figures 1-13 and checked that the plots support circuit variants, phase traces, and spike correlations but not causal claims. Inspected the public PAL repository structure and primary arXiv/OpenReview records for modular-circuit, sparse-function, and training-stability competitors through 2026-08-23.
